findings.claim: KC1 'Which mountain-building period produced the granite tors of Dartmoor?' marks 'Variscan' correct while also offering 'Hercynian' as a distractor.
findings.truth: Hercynian is simply the older name for the Variscan orogeny. A student who picks Hercynian gives a correct answer and is marked wrong. Replacing the distractor with 'Himalayan' leaves one correct option.
findings.evidence: Standard geological nomenclature (Variscan = Hercynian orogeny, ~380-280 Ma)

findings.claim: 'the prevailing easterly storms hit the cliff at an angle that drives strong longshore drift south' (Holderness)
findings.truth: The UK's prevailing winds are south-westerly, as L2 and L7 both state. Holderness is attacked by north-easterly storm waves crossing a long North Sea fetch; those waves, not a 'prevailing easterly' wind, drive drift southwards.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction with L2 and L7; standard Holderness wave climate

findings.claim: Mark scheme for Q5 repeats 'prevailing easterly storms driving longshore drift'.
findings.truth: Same error as F2; the mark scheme must match the corrected text.
findings.evidence: Consistency with F2

findings.claim: 'give a cost or rate where you can (groynes = £5,000-10,000/m ...)'
findings.truth: £5,000-10,000 per metre is the standard cost band for a sea wall, not a groyne. The lesson itself gives a sea wall at about £6,000 per metre, so the tip contradicts its own content.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction with content_html of the same lesson

findings.claim: 'Storm Arwen in November 2021 and Storm Babet in October 2023 brought serious flooding to towns along the Tees including Yarm and Stockton.'
findings.truth: Storm Arwen was a wind and snow storm: gusts to 110 mph, three deaths from falling trees, about 8 million trees damaged in Scotland and mass power cuts. River flooding was not among its impacts. Storm Babet did bring heavy rain and flood warnings to north-east England.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Storm Arwen (impacts section)

findings.claim: 'a flood-relief storage area at Hurworth Burn' protects riverside towns on the Tees.
findings.truth: Hurworth Burn Reservoir is a County Durham water-supply reservoir in the Castle Eden Burn catchment, not a Tees flood-storage scheme, and no such scheme is documented. The Yarm flood defences are real and are kept.
findings.evidence: No source found for a Tees flood storage area of that name; unsupported named scheme removed rather than replaced

findings.claim: At High Force 'the river drops 22 metres'.
findings.truth: The fall at High Force is 21 m (69 ft).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, High Force

findings.claim: 'pyramidal peaks like Helvellyn (950 m)' in the Lake District.
findings.truth: Helvellyn has a broad ridge summit with corries (Red Tarn) and aretes (Striding Edge, Swirral Edge) on its eastern flank. It is not a pyramidal peak; the same lesson correctly gives Snowdon and the Matterhorn as pyramidal peaks. Height of 950 m is correct.
findings.evidence: Definition of a pyramidal peak (three or more corries meeting at a summit); internal contradiction within the lesson

findings.claim: Key Fact repeats 'pyramidal peaks (Helvellyn)'.
findings.truth: Same error as F8; the Key Fact is what students revise from.
findings.evidence: Consistency with F8

findings.claim: 'Llyn Idwal in Snowdonia and Wast Water in the Lake District sit in classic glacial troughs.'
findings.truth: Llyn Idwal is a corrie (cirque) lake in Cwm Idwal, a hanging valley above the Nant Ffrancon trough, so it is the wrong example for a glacial trough. Llyn Ogwen is a ribbon lake in the Nant Ffrancon trough and fits.
findings.evidence: Standard Snowdonia glacial geomorphology

findings.claim: 'Since 1850, average UK temperatures have risen by around 1°C ... six of the warmest UK years on record have happened since 2003.'
findings.truth: The Met Office reports that 2016-2025 was 1.33°C warmer than 1961-1990, so warming since 1850 is more than 1.3°C, and that the ten warmest years in the UK series have all occurred since 2003 (2025 is the warmest, with four of the last five years in the top five).
findings.evidence: Met Office, State of the UK Climate pages (metoffice.gov.uk/research/climate/maps-and-data/about/state-of-climate)

findings.claim: Cyclone Idai: 'Over 1,300 people died and 3 million were displaced.'
findings.truth: More than 3 million people were affected; about 400,000 were displaced (IFRC). Displacement and impact are not the same figure.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Cyclone Idai

findings.claim: 'storm surge' is listed twice with two different definitions.
findings.truth: One duplicate entry should be removed. Both definitions are correct, so no marks are at risk; it only makes the glossary render the term twice.
findings.evidence: Direct inspection of glossary_terms

findings.claim: 'The Lake District seeing 600 mm of rain a year is normal; East Anglia seeing 600 mm is generous'.
findings.truth: The comparison is inverted. The Lake District averages roughly 2,000-3,300 mm a year (L7 says over 3,000 mm and up to 4,000 mm), so 600 mm there would be a severe drought. East Anglia's normal annual rainfall is about 600 mm.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction with L7; standard UK rainfall averages

findings.claim: 'Tropical forests alone store an estimated 250 gigatonnes of carbon - more than humans have emitted from fossil fuels since 1850.'
findings.truth: Cumulative fossil fuel emissions since 1850 are about 1,780 GtCO2, roughly 485 gigatonnes of carbon, so 250 Gt is around half, not more.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere (2,650 GtCO2 from all human activity since 1850); Global Carbon Budget fossil share

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Around 250 gigatonnes - more than humans have emitted since 1850.'
findings.truth: Same error as F15; the flashcard is the version students memorise.
findings.evidence: Consistency with F15

findings.claim: The matching question offers 'Tropical rainforest plant' twice (right[0] and right[2]) as labels for buttress roots and drip tips.
findings.truth: Two identical labels make the key ambiguous: a student who pairs the right words with the other index is marked wrong for a correct answer. Making the two labels distinct (root adaptation / leaf adaptation) fixes it without changing the answer order.
findings.evidence: Direct inspection of knowledge_checks[4]

findings.claim: L13 gives Lake District tourism as 'around £2.3 billion annually and ... roughly 18,000 jobs'; L6 gives 'over 18 million visitors a year bring £1.4 billion to the local economy'.
findings.truth: The two lessons give different values for the same statistic, so a student cannot know which to quote. The National Park Authority's own published pairing is about 18 million visitors, about £1.4 billion and about 18,000 jobs; more recent Cumbria Tourism figures are higher. One figure should be chosen and used in both lessons. I could not settle which without a current published source.
findings.evidence: Internal contradiction between L6 and L13

findings.claim: 'when Haweswater was raised, the village of Mardale Green was submerged without any offer to rehouse the community; today the same tension resurfaced when United Utilities proposed raising the dam again in the 2000s.'
findings.truth: Neither claim is documented. Sources record that Mardale Green and Measand were demolished, the church dismantled and the graves moved to Shap, but say nothing about rehousing arrangements; no 2000s proposal to raise the dam is recorded. Both specifics should be checked before a student quotes them in a case study.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Haweswater Reservoir (silent on both points)

findings.claim: The Black Summer fires 'killed 33 people, three billion animals and burnt 18 million hectares'.
findings.truth: The 33 deaths and 18 million hectares are right. The WWF figure of three billion is animals killed OR displaced, so 'killed' overstates it slightly.
findings.evidence: WWF Australia 2020 report wording

findings.claim: 'In 1983 only 21% of the country was forested' (Costa Rica).
findings.truth: Published series differ: one gives 17% in 1983, another gives 21% at the 1987 low point. The lesson pairs the year from one series with the percentage from the other. The recovery figure of over 60% by 2024 is consistent with FAO data (59.4% in 2020).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Deforestation in Costa Rica (1983 = 17%); commonly published 1987 = 21%

findings.claim: Every one of the 13 lessons carries a '6 marks - Explain Causes & Impacts' practice question, and the exam tips in L2, L6, L7, L8 and L11 coach students for '6-mark questions'.
findings.truth: The spec lists this paper's question types as multiple choice, short open, open response, calculations and 8-mark extended writing, with three 30-mark sections; it names no 6-mark tariff. A 6-mark item is the house form of other boards. I cannot prove from the spec alone that no 6-mark item exists, because 'open response' is not given a tariff. Recommendation: confirm against a real past paper; if the tariffs are only 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8, relabel the 6-mark item as 4 or 8 marks across the whole unit and delete the '6-mark' phrases from the five exam tips. This is a fleet-wide pattern, not a one-unit slip.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/geography-a-1GA0.md assessment overview and assessment information sections

summary: Thirteen lessons checked against the spec and against published figures; 22 findings, 17 of them fixed. The mark-costing errors are a knowledge check with two correct options (L1), a matching key with two identical labels (L12), an inverted UK rainfall comparison (L10), a wrong pyramidal-peak and wrong glacial-trough example (L6), a wind storm described as a flood (L5) and Cyclone Idai's affected count reported as displaced (L9). Two items need Tom's ruling: the Lake District tourism figure, which differs between L6 and L13, and the 6-mark practice tariff that appears in every lesson but not in the spec's list of question types.
